title: Effective hyperuniformity in time-integrated stochastic Turing patterns
abstract: Demographic noise generates stochastic Turing patterns even when reaction-diffusion systems are deterministically stable. We show analytically and verify numerically in the Levin-Segel model that temporal integration of configurations reveals emergent large-scale organization. The intensive number variance in a window of size $R \gg 1$ approaches a finite reaction-kinetic floor as $1/R$, over a spatial range growing by orders of magnitude near the Turing instability. This yields an effectively hyperuniform, fine-tuning-free regime previously unidentified in non-conserved multispecies stochastic systems.
summary: This work analyzes stochastic Turing patterns in reaction-diffusion systems, showing that integrating fluctuations over time reveals a hidden large-scale order. This emergent structure exhibits effective hyperuniformity, meaning long-wavelength density variations are suppressed by a finite kinetic floor. The methodology uses advanced statistical tools like the structure factor analysis within the Linear Noise Approximation.
main_problem: The study investigates how robust, large-scale spatial organization emerges from stochastic Turing patterns when considering time integration of fluctuating local populations.
main_result: Time integration acts as a dynamical filter that reveals an emergent effective hyperuniformity in the density fluctuations, characterized by a $1/R$ decay in variance over intermediate scales.
method: The analysis uses the Linear Noise Approximation (LNA) applied to stochastic reaction-diffusion equations and analyzes the time-integrated structure factor in Fourier space.
model_or_system: The model is a generic two-species stochastic reaction-diffusion process, exemplified by the Levin-Segel predator-prey system, evolving on a lattice with periodic boundary conditions.
key_observables: Time-integrated demographic fluctuations ($\Xi(X)_r(T)$), structure factor $S(X)_q(T)$, and intensive variance $	ext{var}(X)(R; T)$.
important_parameters:
The ratio of diffusion rates ($
u/\mu$) relative to the deterministic instability point, and the integration time $T$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Linear Noise Approximation (LNA) and assumes that the system reaches a steady state for the structure factor in the long-time limit ($T 	o \infty$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the emergence of patterns in time-integrated vs. instantaneous snapshots, showing variance decay as $1/\ell$ over increasingly broad regions near instability.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the mathematical framework using LNA for stochastic fluctuations, derives the structure factor for time-integrated configurations, and then applies this to the Levin-Segel model to demonstrate the transition from instantaneous noise to long-range hyperuniform order.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the concept of emergent organization via filtering (time integration) is analogous to how quantum correlations or entanglement can be revealed by time evolution measurements in open quantum systems.

Left panels (a,d): instantaneous steady-state configurations; middle and right panels (b,e) and (c,f): time-averaged over T = 32 and T = 1024 respectively, revealing how the spatially organized population structure gradually emerges as the integration time increases, absent in any single snapshot. The 2D simulation is shown for visual purposes only; all quantitative analyses are performed on the 1D model.

A peak signals the appearance of a spatial pattern: at ν/µ = 20, the predator shows no discernible peak instantaneously, and it only emerges after time in- tegration, while the prey already shows a peak in both, but with a stronger one after time integration.
